title: Mariners’ dismal week continues with 19-2 loss to Cubs
content:
As the saying goes, you never know what you’re going to see when you attend a baseball game.

That held true after Seattle Mariners center fielder Julio Rodríguez caused reliever José A. Ferrer to open the sixth inning with a 1-0 count.

The reason?

Rodríguez was tossing a baseball into the crowd well after Ferrer ran out of warmup pitches and with Chicago Cubs second baseman Pedro Ramírez ready for his at-bat.

Ramírez singled, then came around to score in what ended up as a 19-2 Mariners loss, one that featured two grand slams and three position players pitching, two of whom were from Seattle.

And yet it’s not the worst loss the Mariners have had this season. It’s not even the worst loss they’ve had in the last week. That honor goes to a 22-0 thrashing by the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday, a loss that tied the modern-era MLB record (since 1900) for the largest shutout.

And like Rodríguez’s club, it’s also not even the worst gaffe by the outfielder this week!

In that 22-0 loss, Rodríguez evidently forgot how many outs there were and tossed a live baseball into the stands of American Family Field, allowing Milwaukee to score its 21st run on what was originally a routine sacrifice fly.

Oddly enough, Sunday’s 19-2 loss and Tuesday’s 22-0 drubbing were both started by Bryce Miller. In each of those games, Miller was pulled before reaching five innings and was tagged for six and five earned runs, respectively. It’s part of a career-worst month for the 28-year-old. Over four starts in August, Miller has allowed 21 runs (20 earned) on 22 hits, with 18 strikeouts against 12 walks (20 innings pitched) for a 9.00 ERA.

That stretch has put Miller’s spot in the rotation into question. With Seattle having called up baseball’s No. 1-ranked prospect, Kade Anderson, the club has six healthy starters on its depth chart. Faced with that conundrum earlier in the season, the club shifted to a piggyback plan in which one starter would come in relief of another.

“We’re looking at all different kind of options as we approach the end of the season here, and looking at everything,” manager Dan Wilson said. “Obviously want to keep our rotation intact, but we’ll see how things shake down here in the next few days.”

As for the rest of the club, despite another memorably lopsided loss, the Mariners are in contention for the AL West crown. At 62-69, Seattle is three games behind the Houston Astros and Texas Rangers for the division lead. The Mariners are also three games out of the AL’s third and final wild-card spot.

It’s the byproduct of a weak year for the American League. At the end of play Sunday, only four clubs had winning records in the AL (Tampa Bay, New York, Boston and Chicago) compared with the NL, where eight teams had records above .500 and a ninth (St. Louis) sat at .500.

In the AL West, things have been particularly ugly with no team in the division having a positive run differential. Seattle’s minus-61 mark ranks third-best in the West.

It’s created a real possibility that, with roughly 31 games left in the season, the winner of the AL West and the third AL wild-card could both have losing records. That’s never occured in a full 162-game campaign.

“I think numbers don’t lie sometimes, and I’d be lying if I said the American League was in a different spot for our own standings,” Blue Jays manager John Schneider said at the All-Star Game when asked about the disparity between MLB’s senior and junior circuits.

As it stands, the 2005 San Diego Padres, who managed to win the NL West with an 82-80 record, stand as the team with the fewest wins to make it to October in the wild-card era. That club was promptly swept in the NLDS by the St. Louis Cardinals. As is the case with this year’s AL West, the 2005 NL West had no team finish with a positive run-differential.

Whether history will be made remains to be seen, but it certainly is leaning that way, and losses like Sunday’s don’t help.
